transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-06-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Maya Lin (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Halo - Head of Security), Ben Ortiz (Halo - Cloud Architect), Sara Lu (Halo - Compliance Manager)

[00:00] Jordan: Thanks for carving out time, everyone. We're here to walk through audit and admin activity capture options for Redwood — especially export and retention that your compliance team needs. Maya and I will take you through current capture surface and then we can deep dive into KMS and SSO stuff.
[00:14] Priya: Thanks Jordan, appreciate it. Just to set context — we're doing internal SOC 2 readiness and Palo Alto asked about offsite retention of admin trails. We're looking for immutable export and evidence that keys are customer controlled where necessary.
[00:28] Maya: Yep, totally — good starting point. Quick run-through of what Redwood captures by default: admin console logins, API key lifecycle events (create/rotate/revoke), model route changes, rollout events, RBAC grant/revoke, SSO logins (SAML/assertions), and operator actions like scale-up, drains, and config changes. We also capture request-level metadata for inference calls: timestamps, model ID, tokens counted, but not PII by default unless you've sent it in prompt — we'll talk about redaction later.
[00:54] Ben: How granular are the admin logs? Like do we get the before/after of a configuration change or just the event that it happened?
[01:05] Maya: We capture both the event and a JSON patch in most cases — so you can see old vs new for things like rollout thresholds or model pins. Occasionally the patch may be truncated for very large blobs — UX thing — but we include a reference to the full artifact stored in the internal log store. That's the part some customers choose to export off-platform for long-term legal retention.
[01:29] Priya: Ok. For SOC 2 we need immutable evidence for a 12 month window with restricted access. How do we support that?
[01:38] Jordan: Two patterns we recommend: short-term retention in Redwood with role-based access and audit policies, and long-term export to your own cloud bucket (S3/GCS/Azure) with server-side encryption and bucket locking enabled. For immutability we support S3 Object Lock-compatible exports. We can also stream logs to your SIEM via Kafka or syslog if you want near-real-time ingestion.
[02:03] Sara: Does Redwood sign the logs or provide a tamper-evidence checksum?
[02:09] Maya: We compute and store SHA-256 digests for log batches and persist them with the event header. If you export them, the digests are included so you can verify integrity after transit. We're working on HSM-backed signing but currently digests plus S3 Object Lock is the common compliance pattern.
[02:26] Ben: On encryption, do we manage keys or can we use customer KMS/HSM?
[02:31] Jordan: Both. Hosted mode has Redwood-managed keys by default. For Dedicated/Private or enterprise customers you can bring your own key (BYOK) via KMS integration — we support AWS KMS (multi-region), GCP KMS, and on-prem HSM via PKCS#11 for private deployments. We key-wrap the log encryption keys with your KMS so Redwood doesn't have plaintext key material for long-term exports.
[02:57] Priya: And rotation? We need quarterly rotation and a documented rotation history.
[03:02] Maya: Our KMS integration supports automatic key rotation. Rotation events are logged with key IDs and timestamps, and we store the previous key metadata so you have a clear chain of custody.
[03:13] Priya: Good. Now about access controls — we have multiple teams and need fine-grained RBAC, especially for who can request exports.
[03:22] Jordan: Redwood's RBAC maps to roles and policies. You can separate export privileges into a specific role. We also support SCIM provisioning so your identity provider can centrally manage group membership. Exports require a multi-step approval flow if enabled — the request shows up in an approval queue and approvers get email/SMS notifications.
[03:44] Ben: Is approval flow customizable? We might want 2 approvers for production exports.
[03:48] Maya: Yes. Approval policies are templated and can enforce n-of-m approvers, timeouts, and audit comments. Everything about who approved is part of the audit trail.
[03:58] Priya: In terms of what's actually in the exported artifact, can we tailor fields? Our legal folks want certain fields and to redact others.
[04:08] Maya: Export templates let you pick a schema. Default includes timestamp, event_type, actor (user id & email), resource, action, before_state (if present), after_state, request_id, and origin IP. You can add custom metadata like correlation_id. For redaction we offer post-ingest processors to mask PII — or you can use pre-export hooks to transform fields. We recommend keeping unredacted logs in your own bucket if you need full fidelity but redacting copies for business use.
[04:40] Sara: If we redact for business use, how do we keep an unredacted canonical for audits but still limit access?
[04:46] Jordan: Keep canonical in a separate bucket with restrictive IAM and S3 Object Lock, and create a derived redacted view in a different bucket or attach a lifecycle that limits read access. We can automate that via the export job, and we can include a manifest with checksums for the canonical copy.
[05:03] Ben: How about retention policies? We need rolling retention: operational logs 90 days, audit evidence 3-7 years depending on region.
[05:13] Maya: The platform supports per-stream retention. You can set short retention for inference telemetry and longer for admin trails. For long-term, we strongly suggest exporting to your archive bucket with lifecycle rules to Glacier/Coldline. We also support configurable deletion windows and legal hold flags.
[05:30] Priya: Data residency — can we force logs originating from EU regions to stay within EU endpoints?
[05:36] Jordan: Yes — region routing policies can pin storage to specific regions. When you provision export targets, you select the target region and Redwood will only write to endpoints in that region. For cross-region replication you'd need explicit approval.
[05:49] Ben: On the streaming side, if we feed logs into our SIEM, do we need to run agents or is it push from Redwood?
[05:56] Maya: Redwood can push via HTTPS/webhook, Kafka, or forward via syslog. We do offer a lightweight agent for edge cases, but push-based integrations are more common. All pushes are authenticated via signed tokens and optional mTLS.
[06:16] Priya: Any SLA around export jobs? For example, guaranteed delivery within X hours?
[06:21] Jordan: For hosted customers we provide best-effort, typically minutes for near-real-time streams, and export jobs for larger historical snapshots run in batch and we provide delivery windows based on size — we'll commit specifics in the Dedicated contract. For compliance POCs we usually run a sample job and confirm end-to-end within agreed window.
[06:42] Sara: We need evidence for the last 6 months — how much data volume should we expect? Our ingress is fairly heavy during policy updates.
[06:49] Ben: Our ops team does a lot of model pinning and config changes, maybe several thousand events a month.
[06:55] Maya: We can estimate. Admin events are low-volume compared to inference tokens — usually tens to hundreds of KB per event. I'll run an estimate off your projected event count and send a sizing doc.
[07:08] Priya: On the topic of dashboards and evidence collection, do you provide pre-built SOC 2 evidence exports?
[07:15] Jordan: We ship a SOC 2 pack — a set of evidence artifacts including config snapshots, rotation logs, export manifests, and selected audit intervals. For the auditor you usually provide the canonical logs and the manifests verifying tamper-evidence.
[07:30] Sara: Great. Any limitations on filters when exporting? e.g., can we export by user or action type?
[07:36] Maya: Yes filters are flexible: time-range, user_id, event_type, resource_id, region, and custom tags. Exports can be incremental (only appended events) to minimize data transfer.
[07:49] Ben: About retention enforcement — suppose a user asks to delete an event under GDPR. If an event is in a write-once bucket with Object Lock, how do you reconcile that with erase requests?
[07:59] Jordan: Good question. For EU data subject requests we recommend storing replicates for audit in an internal legal hold that is separate from personal-data copies. If an erase is required, we will provide an export that omits the subject's personal identifiers and mark the canonical with an access restriction. This is an area we consult on per-case, and it's why many customers keep PII out of logs or tokenize it at ingestion.
[08:29] Priya: For our purposes we want a POC: 1) export admin trails for last 30 days to our S3 with Object Lock enabled and KMS key, 2) show proof of digest/checksum verification, 3) show RBAC controlling who can request the export. Can you do that?
[08:45] Maya: Yes — that aligns with a standard POC. We can run it against a test bucket in your AWS account; we'll need cross-account role details or a pre-signed bucket policy.
[08:57] Ben: I'll set up a test bucket and send role arn to Maya. Any specific IAM permissions you need?
[09:03] Maya: Minimal: s3:PutObject, s3:PutObjectAcl (if needed), kms:Encrypt/kms:GenerateDataKey (for key wrap), and s3:PutObjectTagging if you want manifest tags. We'll send a sample policy.
[09:16] Priya: One more thing — we use Okta for SSO. How does session mapping appear in the logs?
[09:22] Jordan: We ingest SAML attributes like email, subject, groups, and session id. The logs will include assertion_id and the raw assertion reference. Note SAML raw assertions are sensitive, so we redacted full assertion by default but include assertion_id for traceability.
[09:41] Sara: For retention lengths in different jurisdictions, can you make export lifecycle be conditional on region?
[09:47] Maya: Yes, export jobs can be configured per-region and lifecycle rules follow the bucket’s configuration. We can orchestrate per-region export tasks.
[09:56] Priya: Any gap windows where logs are buffered but not yet exported — we need to demonstrate no blind spot.
[10:01] Maya: Buffering exists for retry resilience — default is low minutes, and we surface queue depth metrics in the console. For the POC we'll set low buffer TTL and show the metrics to prove there’s no significant blind spot.
[10:15] Ben: Are there e2e encryption examples we can show to auditors? A document or a diagram?
[10:19] Jordan: Yes — we'll attach an encryption flow diagram, key rotation history sample, and the digest verification steps in the POC pack.
[10:29] Priya: Okay, let's recap next steps.
[10:32] Jordan: Recap: Jordan will send the audit log schema, export policy options, and a sample S3 bucket policy by 2025-06-05. Maya will run the POC export into Halo's test S3, configure KMS wrap, and provide checksum verification steps by 2025-06-09. Sara will confirm required audit fields and any regulatory hold rules by 2025-06-06. We'll schedule a follow-up POC review week of 2025-06-16.
[10:57] Sara: Sounds good, thanks.
[11:00] Ben: Thanks everyone.
[11:03] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links to the docs.
